extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, in-house counsel, and patent applicants in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to respond to obviousness‑type double patenting rejections and how proposed USPTO rule changes to terminal disclaimers would affect claim drafting and portfolio strategy for U.S. patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed terminal disclaimer enforceability condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO proposes that terminal disclaimers can overcome an obviousness‑type double patenting rejection only if the terminal disclaimer ties the subject application's enforceability to the reference application's validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, the proposed rule would require the terminal disclaimer to include an agreement that the subject patent is only enforceable so long as it is not tied “directly or indirectly” to a patent in which “any claim has been finally held unpatentable or invalid as anticipated or obvious by a Federal court in a civil action or by the USPTO, and all appeal rights have been exhausted; or a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on anticipation or obviousness to that claim has been made.” In practice this would make a terminally disclaimed patent unenforceable if the referenced patent has even a single claim found invalid for anticipation or obviousness (with appeals exhausted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing common‑ownership requirement (37 C.F.R. § 1.321(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Current regulation requires that a terminal disclaimer include a provision that the subject patent be enforceable only so long as it and the reference patent are commonly owned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This anti‑harassment provision is intended to prevent different patentees from separately asserting patents with patentably indistinct claims against the same defendant. The proposed rule would add an additional validity‑tying condition on top of this common‑ownership requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness‑type double patenting doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness‑type double patenting is a judicially created doctrine that prohibits obtaining multiple patents with patentably indistinct claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two main policy motivations: (1) prevent patent owners from extending the term of their monopoly by obtaining multiple patents with indistinct claims, and (2) prevent harassment where different patentees could separately assert substantially the same invention. Terminal disclaimers are a common mechanism to address this doctrine by aligning patent term or ownership conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer mechanism and typical content
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer is filed to disclaim a terminal portion of a patent’s term, typically referencing another patent or application so both patents expire on the same day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers commonly (a) disclaim the post‑expiration term of the subject patent based on a reference patent’s expiration date and (b) include the common‑ownership/enforceability clause required by 37 C.F.R. § 1.321(c)(3). Under the proposed rule, they would also need the additional validity‑tying language described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant strategic responses to double patenting rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed rule is enacted, applicants should reconsider whether to file terminal disclaimers and may prefer alternative responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended strategies include: traversing the double patenting rejection (arguing against it), amending claims to overcome the rejection rather than filing a terminal disclaimer, filing earlier family applications with relatively narrow claims, amending more aggressively in earlier applications and progressively broadening in continuation applications, and otherwise managing claim scope across a family to reduce the risk that later applications will be rendered unenforceable by broader earlier applications. The article notes applicants may more strongly consider these options because a terminal disclaimer could link enforceability to another patent’s ultimate invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO policy rationale for proposed change
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO says the proposal aims to reduce litigation costs caused by multiple related patents with very similar scope by tying validity/enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By making related patents’ enforceability interdependent, defendants and patentees could focus validity disputes on a single patent, potentially producing more focused claim construction hearings, lower litigation costs, and faster resolution. The article reports this as the USPTO's justification for the proposed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question about USPTO statutory authority to adopt the change
rubrics_metrics.description: The article questions whether the USPTO has statutory authority to impose new conditions on terminal disclaimers that go beyond regulating the conduct of proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO cites In re Van Ornum (CCPA 1982) as precedent for regulating anti‑alienation clauses, but the article notes Van Ornum relied on a long history addressing harassment concerns and that there is not a similarly clear historical basis for the USPTO to regulate terminal disclaimers based on litigation‑cost concerns. Thus the proposal may face legal challenge as potentially unlawful agency action.
